client: I've been really struggling since I started college last semester — the workload is just so much more than I expected, and I feel like I'm constantly falling behind no matter how hard I try. It's gotten to the point where I've kind of pulled away from the friends I made at the beginning of the year because I feel like I can't afford to socialize when I have so much to catch up on. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the assignments aren't going anywhere.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — feeling perpetually behind while also isolating yourself from the people who could offer some relief is an exhausting cycle to be stuck in. I also hear a bit of skepticism about whether this conversation can help, which makes a lot of sense when the practical pressures feel so concrete and unchanging. I'm curious — when you imagine "catching up," what does that actually look like for you, and do you feel like that moment ever truly arrives?

client: Honestly, when I imagine catching up, it's like... I picture a version of me who finally has an empty inbox, no overdue tasks, no one waiting on something from me. But you're right that I'm not sure that moment ever actually arrives — and when I sit with that, it kind of makes me feel sick, like what's the point of all this grinding if the finish line doesn't exist. I guess I've never really let myself think about it that directly before.
therapist: That image of the "empty inbox" version of you is really revealing — it sounds like you've been running toward a finish line that keeps moving, and letting yourself see that clearly for the first time brings up something that feels almost grief-like. In CBT we'd call that underlying belief a kind of rule you've been living by — that rest or connection is only earned once everything is done — and it's worth gently questioning whether that rule is actually serving you. What do you think that belief has cost you this semester, beyond just the time spent studying?

client: Honestly, when you put it that way — that it's like grief — something kind of clicked, but it also made me feel defensive, like I don't want to admit how much I've lost. I think it's cost me... my friendships, mostly. There were so many times people invited me out and I said no because I had one more chapter to get through, and now those same people have stopped asking. But here's the thing — I'm not sure I fully buy that it's just a "belief" I can question my way out of, because the work really does pile up, and if I'd gone out instead, I'd have fallen behind.
therapist: That defensiveness you're feeling makes complete sense — acknowledging what you've lost with your friendships is genuinely painful, and it takes courage to even name it. You're also raising a really fair point, and I want to honor it: the work *is* real, and I'm not suggesting you could have ignored it. But I'm curious about the times you said no — did saying yes even once actually lead to falling catastrophically behind, or has that consequence mostly lived in anticipation rather than experience?

client: That's... actually a harder question to answer than I expected. When I think back honestly, I can't point to a specific time where I said yes to hanging out and then my work completely fell apart because of it. But the fear of that happening feels so real and so loud that it's almost like the memory of a disaster that never actually occurred.
therapist: What you just noticed is genuinely significant — you've been living under the shadow of a disaster that your own memory can't actually confirm ever happened, and that takes real honesty to see. In CBT, we'd call that a "predictive thought" that's been treated as fact, and the evidence you just examined doesn't really support it. I wonder — if that fear is more of a story your mind has been telling you than a reflection of reality, what might become possible for you this week if you tested it just once?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe it — like, maybe I have been carrying around this story that everyone will leave if I get too close. But then there's this other part of me that says, "Yeah, but what if this is the one time it actually happens?" I guess I could try reaching out to someone this week, but honestly the thought of it already makes my chest tight.
therapist: That tightness in your chest is really worth paying attention to — it tells us just how much this matters to you, and how long you've been bracing for a rejection that may never come. That "what if this is the one time" voice is incredibly common, but notice that it's asking you to pay an ongoing, certain cost — loneliness — to avoid a loss that's only possible, not guaranteed. Who is one person from earlier this year that felt genuinely safe to you, even briefly, and what would a small, low-stakes reach out to them look like?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, there is one person who comes to mind — my old coworker Dani, who I used to eat lunch with before she moved to a different department. But even just thinking about texting her makes me feel this weird preemptive embarrassment, like I'm already imagining her being too busy or not really caring that I reached out. I guess I can see what you mean about paying a certain cost to avoid an uncertain one, but knowing that logically doesn't make the anxiety go away.
therapist: That preemptive embarrassment is so human — your mind is essentially writing Dani's response for her before she's even had the chance to reply, and it's writing a painful one. You're absolutely right that insight doesn't automatically dissolve anxiety, and in CBT we'd say the only thing that really loosens that grip is small, real-world experiments that give your nervous system new data to work with. What do you think a genuinely low-stakes first message to Dani might look like — something that would feel manageable even with the anxiety present?

client: I hear what you're saying about needing real-world data, and part of me gets that logically. But when I try to actually picture typing out a message to Dani, even something casual like "hey, it's been a while," my mind immediately goes to — what if she takes forever to reply, or gives me some short, flat response, and then I'm just sitting there reading into every word? I guess I'm worried that even a "low-stakes" message won't feel low-stakes once I've actually sent it.
therapist: You're naming something really important — that the stakes feel like they shift the moment you press send, because suddenly you're in the waiting, and the waiting is where your mind starts spinning stories. That's not a flaw in the plan; it's actually the exact anxiety pattern worth practicing through, because no amount of preparation fully eliminates that vulnerable moment. I'm wondering — if Dani did reply slowly or briefly, what's the story you'd most likely tell yourself about what that means, and is there another explanation for that same response that would be just as plausible?

client: I'd probably tell myself she's pulling away, or that I said something wrong and now she's regretting being friends with me at all. That's the story that just kind of rushes in automatically, like it's the most obvious explanation even when I know logically it probably isn't. And yeah, I can think of other reasons — she's busy, her phone's in her bag, she's just not a fast texter — but in the moment those feel like excuses I'm making up to calm myself down rather than things I actually believe.
therapist: What you're describing — where the kind explanations feel like "excuses" but the harsh ones feel like truth — is actually a really telling asymmetry, and it points to something worth examining: your mind has been trained to treat self-critical stories as more credible than neutral ones, even when the evidence is equal. That's not a personality flaw; it's a pattern that usually develops for a reason, and it's also one that can shift with practice. I'm curious — when did that automatic story, the one about people pulling away or regretting you, first start feeling like the "obvious" explanation to you?

client: I think it started pretty early, honestly — like, middle school maybe, when I had a group of friends who just kind of... stopped including me one day, and nobody ever explained why. I remember deciding that it must have been something about me, something I did or said, and that explanation just stuck even though I never got any real confirmation. It's weird to think about it now because I can see how that became my default, but knowing that doesn't make it feel any less true when it happens.
therapist: What you just connected is really profound — a younger version of you was left without an explanation and did what any of us would do: filled in the silence with a story that made sense at the time, even if it was unfairly hard on yourself. That story has been so loyal to you, showing up every time there's ambiguity, because it once felt like protection — if you could explain the loss, maybe you could prevent the next one. I'm wondering, if you could speak to that younger version of you who made that decision in middle school, what would you want them to know about why their friends might have drifted that had nothing to do with them?

client: I sit with that for a moment, because it actually hits harder than I expected it to. I think I'd want to tell that kid that middle school is just... chaos, and people are figuring out who they are, and sometimes friendships fall apart because of that, not because you're broken or too much or not enough. But honestly, Luna, even as I say that, there's this voice in the back of my head going, "yeah, but what if it really was you" — like I can say the kind thing out loud and still not fully believe it.
therapist: The fact that you could say that kind thing at all — even with the doubting voice present — is genuinely meaningful, because that compassionate part of you exists even if it doesn't fully have the floor yet. That "yeah, but what if it really was you" voice isn't evidence that the kind version is wrong; it's just a voice that's had a lot more practice and a lot more years of airtime. I'm curious — over the course of our conversation today, has anything shifted, even slightly, in how loud that voice feels compared to when we started?
